questions.question: Why does Antony decide to leave Egypt early in the play?

options.text: Political crises and appeals from Rome require him.
Cleopatra orders him to conquer the Parthians alone.
Caesar has offered to surrender Rome to him.
Octavia has already arrived to take him home.

questions.explanation: Antony says Fulvia's affairs and letters from Roman allies demand his return amid Pompey's challenge.

evidence.exact:
ANTONY.
The business she hath broached in the state
Cannot endure my absence.

ANTONY.
No more light answers. Let our officers
Have notice what we purpose. I shall break
The cause of our expedience to the Queen,
And get her leave to part. For not alone
The death of Fulvia, with more urgent touches,
Do strongly speak to us, but the letters too
Of many our contriving friends in Rome
Petition us at home. Sextus Pompeius
Hath given the dare to Caesar, and commands
The empire of the sea. Our slippery people,
Whose love is never linked to the deserver
Till his deserts are past, begin to throw
Pompey the Great and all his dignities
Upon his son, who, high in name and power,
Higher than both in blood and life, stands up
For the main soldier; whose quality, going on,
The sides o’ th’ world may danger. Much is breeding
Which, like the courser’s hair, hath yet but life
And not a serpent’s poison. Say our pleasure
To such whose place is under us, requires
Our quick remove from hence.

questions.question: Why does Agrippa propose that Antony marry Octavia?

options.text: To remove Lepidus from the alliance immediately.
To bind Antony and Caesar together as family.
To give Pompey control of the Roman fleet.
To make Cleopatra ruler of the Roman provinces.

questions.explanation: Agrippa argues that Octavia's love for both men can hold Antony and Caesar in lasting friendship.

evidence.exact:
AGRIPPA.
To hold you in perpetual amity,
To make you brothers, and to knit your hearts
With an unslipping knot, take Antony
Octavia to his wife; whose beauty claims
No worse a husband than the best of men;
Whose virtue and whose general graces speak
That which none else can utter. By this marriage
All little jealousies, which now seem great,
And all great fears, which now import their dangers,
Would then be nothing. Truths would be tales,
Where now half-tales be truths. Her love to both
Would each to other, and all loves to both,
Draw after her. Pardon what I have spoke,
For ’tis a studied, not a present thought,
By duty ruminated.

questions.question: Why does Pompey reject Menas's plan to kill the Roman leaders aboard his ship?

options.text: He wants Antony to carry out the killings instead.
He has promised to place Menas in Caesar's office.
He will not knowingly sacrifice his honor for power.
He believes the Roman leaders have already escaped.

questions.explanation: Pompey says honor must guide profit; he condemns a murder plan once it has been disclosed to him.

evidence.exact:
MENAS.
These three world-sharers, these competitors,
Are in thy vessel. Let me cut the cable,
And when we are put off, fall to their throats.
All then is thine.

POMPEY.
Show me which way.

evidence.exact:
POMPEY.
Ah, this thou shouldst have done
And not have spoke on ’t! In me ’tis villainy;
In thee ’t had been good service. Thou must know
’Tis not my profit that does lead mine honour;
Mine honour it. Repent that e’er thy tongue
Hath so betray’d thine act. Being done unknown,
I should have found it afterwards well done,
But must condemn it now. Desist, and drink.

questions.question: What does a soldier urge Antony to do before the sea battle?

options.text: Abandon his soldiers and return alone to Rome.
Give Cleopatra command of every Roman legion.
Dismiss the infantry and rely entirely on ships.
Fight on land, where his troops have proved themselves.

questions.explanation: The soldier distrusts ships and reminds Antony that his men have won by fighting on land.

evidence.exact:
SOLDIER.
O noble emperor, do not fight by sea.
Trust not to rotten planks. Do you misdoubt
This sword and these my wounds? Let th’ Egyptians
And the Phoenicians go a-ducking. We
Have used to conquer standing on the earth
And fighting foot to foot.

questions.question: What does Antony do when Cleopatra's ships flee the battle?

options.text: He leaves the fighting and sails after her.
He captures Caesar and ends the battle at once.
He stays behind and takes command of the infantry.
He orders Enobarbus to pursue her while he fights.

questions.explanation: Scarus reports that Antony follows Cleopatra's flight while the sea battle is still in progress.

evidence.exact:
SCARUS.
She once being loofed,
The noble ruin of her magic, Antony,
Claps on his sea-wing and, like a doting mallard,
Leaving the fight in height, flies after her.
I never saw an action of such shame.
Experience, manhood, honour, ne’er before
Did violate so itself.
evidence.prefix:
uld not
Endure a further view.

questions.question: How does Antony respond when he learns Enobarbus has deserted to Caesar?

options.text: He offers Caesar a reward for Enobarbus's capture.
He sends Enobarbus his treasure with kind farewells.
He orders Enobarbus's treasure thrown into the sea.
He has Enobarbus's messengers executed at once.

questions.explanation: Antony orders that none of Enobarbus's possessions be withheld and sends friendly parting words.

evidence.exact:
ANTONY.
Go, Eros, send his treasure after. Do it.
Detain no jot, I charge thee. Write to him—
I will subscribe—gentle adieus and greetings.
Say that I wish he never find more cause
To change a master. O, my fortunes have
Corrupted honest men! Dispatch.—Enobarbus!

questions.question: How does Antony's generosity affect Enobarbus after his desertion?

options.text: It makes him eager to lead Caesar's attack.
It persuades him that Antony never valued him.
It fills him with remorse and a desire to die.
It convinces him to demand still more money.

questions.explanation: Enobarbus sees Antony's bounty as undeserved payment for betrayal and cannot bear to fight against him.

evidence.exact:
ENOBARBUS.
I am alone the villain of the earth,
And feel I am so most. O Antony,
Thou mine of bounty, how wouldst thou have paid
My better service, when my turpitude
Thou dost so crown with gold! This blows my heart.
If swift thought break it not, a swifter mean
Shall outstrike thought, but thought will do’t, I feel.
I fight against thee! No, I will go seek
Some ditch wherein to die; the foul’st best fits
My latter part of life.

questions.question: What false message does Cleopatra send Antony from the monument?

options.text: That Caesar has agreed to surrender to him.
That Octavia has sailed back to Alexandria.
That Enobarbus has captured the Roman camp.
That she has killed herself calling his name.

questions.explanation: Cleopatra instructs Mardian to report her suicide and say her last word was Antony's name.

evidence.exact:
CLEOPATRA.
To th’ monument!
Mardian, go tell him I have slain myself.
Say that the last I spoke was “Antony”,
And word it, prithee, piteously. Hence, Mardian,
And bring me how he takes my death.—To th’ monument!

questions.question: What does Eros do when Antony orders him to kill his master?

options.text: He kills himself rather than strike Antony.
He kills Cleopatra and returns to Antony.
He arrests Antony on Caesar's orders.
He sends Antony into battle unarmed.

questions.explanation: Eros turns his sword on himself to escape the sorrow of killing Antony.

evidence.exact:
EROS.
Why, there then! [kills himself]
Thus do I escape the sorrow
Of Antony’s death.

questions.question: Why does Cleopatra choose death by the asp rather than life under Caesar?

options.text: She hopes the bite will force Antony to return.
She fears being displayed and humiliated in Rome.
She believes the asp will heal her battle wounds.
She wants to fulfill a promise to marry Caesar.

questions.explanation: Cleopatra imagines Roman crowds and actors degrading her, then uses the asp to escape that fate.

evidence.exact:
Now, Iras, what think’st thou?
Thou an Egyptian puppet shall be shown
In Rome as well as I. Mechanic slaves
With greasy aprons, rules, and hammers shall
Uplift us to the view. In their thick breaths,
Rank of gross diet, shall we be enclouded,
And forced to drink their vapour.
[To an asp, which she applies to her breast.]
